value.overview: The Turkey Vulture (Cathartes aura) is a widespread scavenging bird of the Americas. It is recognized by its red, featherless head, long wings, dark body, and pale flight feathers that create a two-toned pattern when seen from below. It commonly soars with its wings held in a shallow V and uses its excellent sense of smell to locate carrion. Turkey Vultures are important natural recyclers, helping remove dead animals from the environment.
value.classification: The Turkey Vulture belongs to the New World vulture family Cathartidae and the order Cathartiformes. Its scientific name is Cathartes aura.
value.identification: This is a large, long-winged vulture measuring about 64–81 cm in length, with a wingspan commonly around 1.7–1.8 m. Adults have a bare reddish head, a dark brown to blackish body, and grayish flight feathers that look silvery along the trailing edges from below. In flight, the wings are held in a noticeable shallow V and the bird often wobbles or tilts while soaring. Juveniles have darker, less distinctly red heads.
value.rangeHabitat: The Turkey Vulture ranges from southern Canada and the United States through Mexico, Central America, and much of South America, including many Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica it is a regular and widespread bird, occurring in lowlands, foothills, open country, pasture, agricultural areas, forest edges, roadsides, and around settlements. It uses broad landscapes where rising air supports soaring and where carrion is available. Roosts and nest sites are usually associated with trees, cliffs, caves, or secluded structures.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rica supports resident Turkey Vultures as well as passage migrants. Large numbers of northern birds move through the country during migration, especially along Caribbean and other major raptor-migration routes, while some individuals remain year-round. Migrants generally soar overhead and rarely land except to roost or during poor weather.
value.breeding: Turkey Vultures do not build a typical nest. They lay one or two eggs on the ground or on a simple surface in sheltered sites such as caves, rock crevices, hollow trees, dense vegetation, or abandoned buildings. Both adults incubate the eggs and feed the young by regurgitation. In Costa Rica, breeding may occur among resident birds where suitable secluded nest sites and year-round food are available, although many Turkey Vultures seen there are migrants or nonbreeding visitors.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on carrion, including dead mammals, birds, reptiles, and other animals. It often finds carcasses by smell as well as sight, an unusual ability among birds of prey. Turkey Vultures frequently forage over roads, pasture, forest margins, beaches, wetlands, and agricultural land. They may gather at large carcasses and commonly feed alongside other vultures, using their relatively weak bill to eat soft tissues.
value.behavior: Turkey Vultures are highly adapted for soaring. They use thermals and wind currents to travel with little wingbeat, sometimes forming large flocks during migration. They roost communally and may spread their wings to warm themselves or dry them. The species is generally nonaggressive and relies on its strong digestive system to process decaying food. When threatened, especially at close range, it may regurgitate partially digested food as a deterrent.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
